answer.label: Not Henry David Thoreau — a 1970s poster line
answer.authorName: J. Richard Lessor (per the Walden Woods Project) — not Thoreau
answer.authorDates: Modern wording popularized on 1970s posters · underlying metaphor dates to 1848
answer.sourceLine: Thoreau never wrote this. The butterfly-and-happiness image goes back to an anonymous 1848 newspaper filler signed only “L,” and the exact modern wording surfaced on motivational posters in the 1970s. The Walden Woods Project credits the modern phrasing to social worker and speaker J. Richard Lessor, though Quote Investigator found it circulating unattributed on 1973 library posters. Either way, it is not Thoreau’s.

source.excerpt: Happiness is like a butterfly: the more you chase it, the more it will elude you, but if you turn your attention to other things, it will come and sit softly on your shoulder.
trail: Quote Investigator traces the butterfly-happiness image to an anonymous item signed “L” in The Daily Crescent (New Orleans) in June 1848, and finds the attribution to Thoreau “unsupported.”

The Walden Woods Project’s Thoreau mis-quotation page lists this line as “erroneously attributed to both Thoreau and Nathaniel Hawthorne,” crediting the modern wording to J. Richard Lessor and 1970s Argus Communications posters.
Quote Investigator found the expanded modern phrasing on 1973 library posters with “no attribution”; the Thoreau credit only appears online around 2012.
source.excerptNote: The 1848 ancestor read very differently: “HAPPINESS.—A butterfly, which when pursued, seems always just beyond your grasp; but if you sit down quietly, may alight upon you.”

source.rightsNote: The exact modern wording is a 20th-century creation — it spread on 1970s Argus Communications posters and is credited to J. Richard Lessor, so it is well past the pre-1931 public-domain cutoff. (The unrelated 1848 “L” ancestor is public domain, but that is not the wording quoted here.) Authorship of the modern line is contested, so treat the rights holder as uncertain but assume it is in copyright.

author.name: J. Richard Lessor
author.heading: Who really wrote it?
author.metaLine: 20th century · American social worker, author & motivational speaker
author.bio: J. Richard Lessor was an American social worker, author, and speaker to whom the Walden Woods Project attributes the modern “butterfly” wording, which spread on motivational posters produced by Argus Communications in the 1970s. The quote does not appear in any of his published books, and the underlying image — happiness as a butterfly that eludes pursuit but alights when you sit quietly — is far older, tracing to an anonymous 1848 newspaper item. Neither Thoreau nor Nathaniel Hawthorne, the two authors most often credited, wrote it.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution trail
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most persistently misattributed feel-good lines. It is pinned on two 19th-century New England authors who never wrote it.

items.why: Attributions to Thoreau are recent — appearing online only around 2012 — and rest on no primary source. Quote Investigator calls the Thoreau linkage unsupported, and the Walden Woods Project lists it as a known Thoreau mis-quotation.

Hawthorne wrote about happiness using a different image (a wild-goose chase, no butterfly). Per Quote Investigator, the butterfly line was juxtaposed with a Hawthorne passage in an 1891 reference work, and readers wrongly fused the two.

misattribution.truthLine: The image originates in an anonymous 1848 newspaper filler signed “L,” and the exact modern wording is a 1970s poster line the Walden Woods Project credits to J. Richard Lessor — not Thoreau or Hawthorne.

context.heading: Why the mix-up sticks
lead: The saying pairs a comforting paradox — chase happiness and it flees; ignore it and it lands — with a gentle nature image, exactly the register readers associate with Thoreau’s Walden. That surface fit is why the misattribution spreads faster than the correction.
In reality the butterfly metaphor is a piece of anonymous 1848 newspaper wisdom that was reworded over more than a century, reaching its familiar modern form on 1970s motivational posters.
context.pull: Chase it and it flees; look away and it lands — a 19th-century newspaper aphorism, not a line from Walden.
